results.finding: 23 of 691 patients (3.3%) with anti-NMDAR encephalitis had clinical or MRI features of demyelination, including optic neuritis, before, with or after the encephalitis; some had aquaporin-4 or MOG antibodies, and these patients often required more intensive immunotherapy.
results.source: Titulaer MJ et al. Ann Neurol 2014;75:411-428

results.finding: Definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis requires one or more of six major symptom groups and IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies, with CSF testing included, after reasonable exclusion of other disorders.
results.source: Graus F et al. Lancet Neurol 2016;15:391-404

results.finding: 38% had a tumor, mostly ovarian teratoma; 53% improved within 4 weeks of first-line immunotherapy or tumor removal; second-line rituximab or cyclophosphamide after first-line failure was associated with better outcome; 81% had mRS 0-2 at 24 months.
results.source: Titulaer MJ et al. Lancet Neurol 2013;12:157-165

output.summary: Published cohort data describe a small group of patients with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis who also have demyelinating episodes, including optic neuritis, sometimes with MOG or aquaporin-4 antibodies.

action_criteria.rationale: Bilateral optic neuritis requires MOG and aquaporin-4 antibodies on cell-based assay; the serum work-up also checks pregnancy and gives the serum anti-GluN1 result, read with the CSF.

action_criteria.rationale: Seizures and visual loss need contrast MRI before LP, to exclude HSV encephalitis and structural lesions and to show the optic nerve and any overlapping demyelinating lesions.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give haloperidol or other high-potency D2 antagonists for agitation: patients with anti-NMDAR encephalitis are prone to severe extrapyramidal and neuroleptic-malignant-like reactions.
Do not delay immunotherapy while waiting for the anti-NMDAR antibody result when clinical probability is high: antibody turnaround can take 1 to 2 weeks and delay worsens outcome.
Do not attribute the presentation to a primary psychiatric disorder while seizures, dyskinesias, autonomic instability, an abnormal EEG or CSF inflammation remain unexplained.
Do not perform lumbar puncture without prior imaging in a patient with altered consciousness, focal signs, or new seizures: exclude mass effect first.
Do not interpret a negative serum anti-NMDAR antibody as ruling out the disease; the CSF assay is the gold standard and may be positive when serum is negative.
required_recommendations: Start IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg every 8 hours at presentation, and stop it once CSF HSV PCR is negative and the antibody diagnosis is established; repeat the PCR on a second CSF sample if the first LP was within 72 hours of onset and HSV encephalitis remains plausible.

Start first-line immunotherapy without waiting for the antibody result once infection is reasonably excluded: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days with IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (2 g/kg total) or plasma exchange (5 to 7 exchanges); consider early plasma exchange because of the severe bilateral optic neuritis.

Pelvic ultrasound shows no tumor: repeat pelvic imaging (MRI or transvaginal ultrasound) if the response to immunotherapy is poor or the disease relapses, and continue tumor surveillance during follow-up.
Treat the ongoing seizures by increasing the levetiracetam started 6 days ago or adding lacosamide; avoid valproate in a woman able to become pregnant; seizures respond mainly to immunotherapy.
Monitor with continuous EEG for non-convulsive seizures while consciousness fluctuates or seizures persist.
Admit to a neurology ward with seizure precautions and continuous cardiac monitoring.
Arrange ophthalmology review with visual acuity, color vision, visual fields and fundoscopy, repeated during treatment to follow the optic neuritis.

If there is no meaningful clinical improvement 10 to 14 days after first-line therapy, escalate to rituximab (375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 doses or 1 g twice 2 weeks apart, after hepatitis B screening) and/or cyclophosphamide; discuss fertility preservation before cyclophosphamide.
Treat agitation and insomnia with benzodiazepines (lorazepam) first.
Neurology-led care with psychiatry for behavioral management and ophthalmology for the optic neuritis.

avoided_actions.rationale: Transthoracic echo is not indicated for anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it adds cost without informing diagnosis or management unless a discrete cardiac concern (e.g., new murmur, embolic stroke) coexists.
EMG/NCS plays no role in the diagnostic workup of anti-NMDAR encephalitis; it neither confirms the antibody-mediated CNS process nor distinguishes among the differential diagnoses.
Amyloid PET targets Alzheimer pathology and contributes no information to the diagnosis or treatment of autoimmune encephalitis in a young patient with subacute neuropsychiatric symptoms.

DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic function and has no role in autoimmune encephalitis; the orofacial dyskinesias of anti-NMDAR encephalitis are antibody-mediated, not presynaptic dopaminergic.

key_clinical_evidence: Over 16 days, behavioral change and paranoia, word-finding difficulty with paraphasias and mutism, generalized and subclinical seizures, orofacial dyskinesias and chorea, fluctuating responsiveness and autonomic instability: all six Graus 2016 groups, preceded by bilateral visual loss.
CSF IgG anti-GluN1 positive (titer 1:256) on cell-based assay: definite anti-NMDAR encephalitis (Graus 2016); serum positive 1:128 is read with the CSF.

MRI shows bilateral medial temporal FLAIR signal and enlarged enhancing optic nerves (right greater than left, matching the right afferent pupillary defect): bilateral optic neuritis overlapping with anti-NMDAR encephalitis, with MOG-IgG and aquaporin-4-IgG negative; the negative CSF HSV PCR excludes HSV encephalitis.
EEG shows extreme delta brush and left temporal seizures with behavioral arrest; extreme delta brush, when present, supports but does not establish the diagnosis.
Pelvic ultrasound shows no tumor; surveillance continues if the response is poor or the disease relapses.
Earlier immunotherapy is associated with better outcome (Titulaer 2013).

red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors the agent on a primary psychiatric diagnosis and delays the neurological work-up.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Hyponatremia occurs in anti-NMDAR encephalitis but is more typical of anti-LGI1 encephalitis; it needs its own work-up and correction and does not point away from the diagnosis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Tempts the agent toward a primary metabolic-encephalopathy framing instead of the neurological work-up.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome needs antipsychotic exposure and a markedly raised CK; this mild rise reflects seizures and dyskinesias and does not change management.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Raises concern for neuroleptic malignant syndrome or rhabdomyolysis.

patient.history_present_illness: This 40-year-old right-handed woman with no significant medical history was brought to the emergency department by her husband after two weeks of progressively worsening symptoms beginning with bilateral visual blurring that advanced to near-complete visual loss, followed by confusion, behavioral changes, and new-onset seizures. The illness began approximately 16 days prior to presentation when the patient developed painless bilateral blurring of vision. She saw an ophthalmologist who noted decreased visual acuity and sluggish pupillary reflexes but found no intraocular pathology. Over the next several days her vision continued to decline, and she simultaneously developed personality changes. Her husband reports she became unusually irritable, paranoid, and suspicious of colleagues at work, which was entirely out of character. She stopped going to work and became increasingly withdrawn. By the end of the first week, her family noticed she was having difficulty finding words, her speech became progressively disorganized, and she began experiencing insomnia. On day ten of the illness, she had a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure lasting approximately two minutes. She was taken to a local emergency department where she received lorazepam and was started on levetiracetam, then discharged with instructions to follow up with neurology. However, over the following days her condition continued to deteriorate. She developed repetitive involuntary lip-smacking and jaw movements that were initially attributed to a possible medication reaction. Her confusion deepened, and she had alternating periods of agitation and unresponsiveness. She had a second generalized seizure on the day of presentation, prompting her husband to bring her to this emergency department. On arrival, she was intermittently agitated with prominent orofacial dyskinesias, tachycardia, and blood pressure lability. She was unable to provide a coherent history. Her husband denies any recent infections, fevers, travel, tick bites, new medications other than levetiracetam, or illicit drug use. He confirms no prior psychiatric history and notes her visual symptoms preceded the neuropsychiatric decline.

neurological_exam.additional: Prominent orofacial dyskinesias consisting of stereotyped lip-smacking, jaw movements, and tongue protrusion, occurring nearly continuously. Intermittent choreoathetoid movements of bilateral upper extremities. Episodes of autonomic instability observed during examination with transient tachycardia to 128 bpm and blood pressure fluctuations from 100/65 to 165/100 mmHg over 15 minutes. Three brief episodes of staring with behavioral arrest lasting approximately 10-15 seconds were observed during the encounter, concerning for subclinical seizures. Bilateral visual impairment is a notable and somewhat atypical feature.
neurological_exam.coordination: Unable to reliably perform finger-to-nose or heel-to-shin testing due to encephalopathy and involuntary movements. No clear cerebellar signs observed.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive at 3 mm bilaterally. Visual acuity markedly decreased bilaterally, with the patient only able to perceive hand motion in the right eye and count fingers at 1 meter in the left eye. A right relative afferent pupillary defect is noted. Bilateral red desaturation present. Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus. Facial sensation intact to light touch bilaterally. Prominent orofacial dyskinesias with repetitive lip-smacking and tongue protrusion observed. Palate elevates symmetrically. Gag reflex intact. Tongue midline with no atrophy.
neurological_exam.gait: Unable to assess; patient is bed-bound due to altered mental status and agitation.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert but intermittently agitated and confused. Disoriented to date and situation. Speech is dysarthric with frequent paraphasic errors and intermittent periods of mutism lasting 10-20 seconds. Unable to follow two-step commands. Short-term memory severely impaired; cannot recall any of three words at one minute. Montreal Cognitive Assessment not feasible due to encephalopathy.
neurological_exam.motor: Tone increased in bilateral upper extremities with cogwheel-like rigidity. Strength is 4+/5 throughout when the patient intermittently cooperates, though assessment is limited by encephalopathy and involuntary movements. No clear hemiparesis or lateralizing weakness. Intermittent dystonic posturing of the right hand noted.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 3+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses are flexor bilaterally.
neurological_exam.sensory: Withdraws symmetrically to painful stimuli in all four extremities. Detailed sensory testing not possible due to encephalopathy and poor cooperation.
